items.headline: SpaceX catches a returning Starship in the tower arms for the first time
items.summary: On Flight 15, Ship 42 came back from orbit to Starbase, Texas and was caught by the launch tower's "chopsticks," the first-ever Starship tower catch. Elon Musk shared a video he said "gives a clear sense of the catch maneuver" and later phone videos he took from the tower. @wintonARK calls it the largest object ever safely returned from orbit and argues it drops the cost per kilogram to orbit to roughly $100, from $1,000. @sriramk: "a testament to what mankind can accomplish."
items.short: Ship 42 returns from orbit and is caught by the tower on Flight 15.

items.headline: Judge lets DRAM antitrust suit against Samsung, SK hynix and Micron go ahead
items.summary: A federal court in California found the plaintiffs plausibly allege that Samsung, SK hynix and Micron agreed to restrict DRAM supply, and denied the companies' motion to dismiss, @jukan05 reports. He calls it a stretch: asking customers to verify end demand, he argues, was meant to stop resellers double-booking orders, not collusion. Separately, Korean media report SK hynix plans to add at least 20,000 wafers a month of HBM4 capacity, citing strong demand from AMD and Broadcom.
items.short: DRAM supply-restriction suit survives a motion to dismiss; SK hynix adds HBM4 capacity.

items.headline: Gene Munster: Nvidia may not give guidance when it reports Tuesday night
items.summary: @munster_gene gives two reasons Nvidia may skip guidance: management changes make it hard for the new CFO to own the forecast, and tighter US Commerce restrictions could put Asia sales at risk, by his estimate about 10% of revenue (China and Hong Kong 8%, other 2%), with some estimates as high as 20%. He says that could pressure the shares next week.
items.short: Munster flags a possible no-guidance print from Nvidia on Tuesday.

items.author: The Humanoid Hub
items.text:
OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team and reassigned the researchers to its general AI teams, even as it keeps building its own humanoid robot, with a first public demo targeted for 2027.

The move, first reported in a Fortune exclusive, is framed by OpenAI as acceleration, not retreat. A spokesperson said "robotics remains a core part of OpenAI's long-term vision," and that the company "remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world."

The real shift is the bet underneath it: that general-purpose models can run robots directly, with no specialized "robot brain" needed. In an Nvidia study, an agent powered by OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra hit 74.8% on a simulated manipulation benchmark, vs 51.0% for the best specialized robotics models.

If that holds, it challenges the premise many robotics startups raised billions on: that robots need brains of their own.

items.author: Serenity
items.text:
The most interesting lesson Jensen Huang taught me

And gave PTSD to Google executives over from his leadership at $NVDA:

Was that if a critical material can be bought out for spare change eg. ~$400m (FY2028 Photonics-SOI revenue forecast for $SOI)

And trigger tens of billions in economic impact to competitors for not securing supply:

We're going to see game theory bottleneck supply procurement actually accelerate upstream through 2027, with or without him. 

I see Morgan Stanley's list highlighting CCL, ABF, PCBs, optical module components as interesting. 

However; I'd put it through my own narrower lens, especially focusing on smaller component cost chokepoints + bottlenecks that doesn't cost much to secure capacity over. 

Deleveraging/negative sentiment is indiscriminately moving the theme up and down together, so hard to argue individual fundamentals at this point. 

Reflecting on 2026, I also prob need to be more selective of companies entering 2027:

But there's going to be a lot of outsized opportunities in bottlenecks... as new architectures like NPO/CPO emerge across the ecosystem.

items.title: It's not Dotcom. It's not 2008. It's Both
items.author: Avian Capital
items.summary: A self-described former bull lays out a bear case for the AI cycle, arguing it combines the dotcom bubble's euphoria over a real technology with 2008-style financing risk. The core claim: the labs sold a winner-take-all race to AGI, but models are turning into a commodity, with buyers barely able to tell suppliers apart, cheap switching and new supply arriving weekly. Worth reading as the strongest version of the other side, whatever your view.

items.title: Mark Zuckerberg used to end meetings by shouting: Domination!
items.author: David Senra
items.summary: Senra collects stories of Zuckerberg's lifelong "emperor mindset": Sean Parker told him to stop ending meetings with "Domination!" because it could surface in an antitrust suit, and he still recites Virgil's Aeneid from high-school Latin. In Facebook's early days he would shout "Carthage must be destroyed!" A short portrait of how a founder's teenage obsessions shape the company.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.
items.explanation: E could hide something that breaks the rule; 3 breaks it if the other side turns out to be E. 4 can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and K isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.
